title: French

description: Immerse yourself in French culture with Parisian elegance, café dialogue, and fluent pronunciation secrets.

proverbOfDay.proverb: Petit à petit, l'oiseau fait son nid.
proverbOfDay.translation: Little by little, the bird builds its nest.
proverbOfDay.context: A classic French reminder of the power of patient consistency: daily language practice yields lasting fluency and deep cultural connection.

cultureTips.title: The Sacred Greeting: Always Say 'Bonjour'
cultureTips.description: In France, entering any bakery, boutique, taxi, or elevator without an audible 'Bonjour' is considered a serious social blunder. 'Bonjour' is not just a greeting; it is the polite pass-key that acknowledges the other person's humanity.

cultureTips.title: The 'Tu' vs 'Vous' Boundary
cultureTips.description: French draws a strict line between intimacy and respect. Use 'Vous' with shopkeepers, elders, strangers, and professional colleagues. Switch to 'Tu' only when invited ('On peut se tutoyer ?') or among close friends and peers.

cultureTips.title: The Art of 'La Bise' (Cheek Kissing)
cultureTips.description: When greeting friends and family, the French exchange cheek kisses (air kisses making a soft kiss sound while touching cheeks). The count varies by region: 2 kisses in Paris, 3 in Montpellier, and 4 in parts of Normandy.

cultureTips.title: Whisper Volume on Public Transit
cultureTips.description: The Paris Métro and regional trains are shared sanctuaries of calm. Speaking loudly, shouting on phones, or playing music without headphones is deeply frowned upon. Keep voices measured and considerate.

cultureTips.title: Casual Elegance over Gym Wear
cultureTips.description: The French default dress code is smart casual ('BCBG' or relaxed chic). Sweatpants, gym attire, and flip-flops are strictly reserved for the gym, home, or beach, and rarely worn on city streets or in restaurants.

cultureTips.title: The Departure Courtesy: 'Merci, Au Revoir'
cultureTips.description: When leaving any small shop, bakery, or post office, it is customary to call out 'Merci, bonne journée, au revoir !' to the cashier or shopkeeper, maintaining the social circle of respect.

lessons.title: Lesson 1: French Alphabet, Accents & Sounds
lessons.description: Master the French alphabet, essential accents (é, è, ê, ç), and key pronunciation secrets like silent final letters.

questions.prompt: How is the acute accent (l'accent aigu: 'é') pronounced in French?
questions.explanation: The accent aigu ('é') produces a crisp, closed sound like 'ay' in English (e.g. 'café', 'été').

questions.prompt: Match the French accents with their names:
Listen to the word 'Français'. Why does the 'c' have a cedilla (ç)?
options: To make the 'c' sound like a soft 's' before 'a'
To show the word is plural
questions.correctAnswer: To make the 'c' sound like a soft 's' before 'a'
questions.explanation: The cédille ('ç') softens the letter 'C' to an 'S' sound in front of A, O, or U.

questions.prompt: In general, what happens to final consonants (like -d, -s, -t, -x) in French words?
questions.explanation: In French, final consonants like 's' in 'Paris' or 't' in 'chat' are usually silent unless liaison occurs.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Salutations & Courtesies
lessons.description: Master essential greetings, polite requests, and daily social etiquette in France.

questions.prompt: What is the universal French greeting used throughout the day?
questions.explanation: 'Bonjour' (Good day / Hello) is the fundamental polite greeting in France.

questions.prompt: Match French greetings with their English meanings:
Listen to the phrase. What does it mean?
questions.explanation: 'S'il vous plaît' is the polite form of 'Please'.
'De rien' is the most common way to say 'You're welcome' in French.
